title: Letters, speeches and articles
specPoints: Paper 2 Section B: the forms the task names, and their conventions; Year 9 letter writing

tips.title: The form is the first decision
tips.body: Article, letter or speech: read it off the task before planning. The form decides the first line, how the reader is addressed, the rhythm and the ending, and the register is judged from the first line.

tips.title: Sincerely for a name, faithfully for Sir or Madam
tips.body: Dear Mrs Okafor takes Yours sincerely; Dear Sir or Madam takes Yours faithfully. The pairing is one of the few layout conventions the examiners notice, because it is heard as register.

tips.title: Seams that earn nothing
tips.body: Addresses and dates on a letter, subheadings every four lines in an article, stage directions in a speech. The conventions that count are the ones a reader hears; the rest cost time.

tips.title: Same plan, different clothes
tips.body: A position, two reasons, the counter-argument met, an ending that asks: the plan is the same in every form. Only the surface changes, so plan the argument and then dress it.

tips.title: Who does it sound as if it is for?
tips.body: Read the first paragraph and answer. A magazine's students, one head teacher, a room of your year: if the answer is the examiner, the register is nobody's and the piece starts again.

tips.title: A speech has no Dear
tips.body: It opens by addressing the room and closes with a call the room repeats. No greeting, no sign-off, no title, no stage directions: the words are the whole performance.

why.matters: Form is how a reader knows what they are holding, and it is the first thing the exam judges, because a writer who does not know whether they are writing a letter, an article or a speech does not yet know who they are talking to. The conventions are small and the effect is large: a title and a request in the first paragraph make a head teacher read on; a headline and a hook make a stranger start; a room addressed in the first line stays addressed. Learning the three forms is learning three ways of standing in front of a reader, and the same argument, dressed for each, is the whole of Paper 2 Section B.

examples.title: The letter that reaches the right desk
examples.body: A complaint to a company, a request to a council, a case to a landlord: each is read by someone who decides in the first paragraph whether to read the second. The exam letter's habits, the title, the purpose and the request before anything else, the courtesy that stays firm, the sign-off that matches the greeting, are the habits that get a real letter answered rather than filed.

examples.title: Standing up in a room
examples.body: A best man, a team captain, a student speaking to governors, someone at a funeral: all are writing a speech, and all face the same problem the exam speech faces, that the room cannot look back and must be told where it is. The habit of addressing the room in the first line, signposting the turns and ending on a sentence the room can repeat is the habit that makes a speech land, and it is learned by writing them.

steps.title: The task names a form, and the form has conventions
steps.body:
The specification says the Paper 2 writing task will specify audience, purpose and form; it does not name the forms themselves. Across series the task has asked for an article, a letter or a speech. June 2024 asked for an article for a school or college magazine.

**Why the form matters.** The AO5 descriptors ask for tone, style and register matched to purpose and audience, and for structural features used with intent. The form supplies both: an article has a headline and a first paragraph that hooks; a letter has a greeting, a purpose stated early and a sign-off; a speech addresses a room and signposts its turns. A piece that ignores its form has mismatched its register before its first sentence.

**What the form does not change.** The argument underneath: a position, reasons, the counter-argument met, an ending that asks. The forms are different clothes on the same body.

**What the examiners do not want.** Addresses and dates laid out at the top of a letter, a page of subheadings in an article, stage directions in a speech. The conventions that matter are the ones the reader hears.

rows: A headline; a standfirst or a hooking first line; paragraphs that build; a closing line
Set by the publication: a school magazine, a broadsheet, a website
A greeting; the purpose in the first paragraph; a sign-off that matches the greeting
Set by the reader: formal to a stranger or an official, warmer to someone known
Address to the room; signposting; a closing call; no greeting or sign-off
Spoken: direct, rhythmic, with the audience as you
Rarer: an essay argues in paragraphs without a headline; a leaflet informs in sections
Formal for the essay; plain and practical for the leaflet

steps.title: The article
steps.body:
An article is written for a publication, and the publication decides the voice. The June 2024 task named a school or college magazine; a task might name a broadsheet newspaper, a local paper or a website.

**The headline.** Short, and promising the argument: not the topic but the position. *Choose the job, not the car* beats *Careers*.

**The first paragraph.** A hook that puts the reader in a picture or a question, and the position within it. A standfirst, one sentence under the headline summarising the piece, is a real convention and can be used, but the hook is what earns.

**The body.** Paragraphs that argue, each one move; a subheading or two is acceptable in a long article, but four subheadings in a page is a leaflet.

**The ending.** A closing line that returns or asks. Articles do not conclude; they land.

**The register.** A school magazine: quick, wry, a shared world, *you* and *we*. A broadsheet: measured, reasoned, the reader assumed to be an adult who wants to be convinced rather than entertained.

steps.title: The letter
steps.body:
A letter is written to one reader, and the reader decides the register. The exam letter is usually to someone with power over the issue: a head teacher, a council, a newspaper's editor, a company.

**The greeting.** *Dear Mrs Okafor* to a named person; *Dear Sir or Madam* to an unknown one; *Dear Editor* to a newspaper. The greeting sets the register, and it must be matched at the end.

**The purpose, first.** The first paragraph says why the letter is written and what it asks for: *I am writing about the proposal to end the school day at half past two, and to ask you to reconsider it.* A reader with power reads the first paragraph and decides whether to read the rest.

**The body.** The argument, in paragraphs that argue: reasons, the counter-argument met, courteously. A letter can be firm without being rude, and the examiners read rudeness as a register lost.

**The sign-off.** *Yours sincerely* to a named person, *Yours faithfully* to Sir or Madam, and a name. No address blocks and dates at the top: they earn nothing and cost time.

**The Year 9 letter.** The school teaches letter writing in Year 9 with the same criteria, and the habits carry: purpose first, the reader's title, the matching sign-off.

steps.title: The speech
steps.body:
A speech is written to be heard, and everything about its register follows from that. The exam speech is usually to a room the writer belongs to: a year group, an assembly, a class, a club.

**No greeting, no sign-off.** A speech opens by addressing the room and closes by asking something of it. *Dear Year 11* is a letter; *Year 11, put your hands up if …* is a speech.

**Address and signposting.** *You* and *we*, often. *I want to make three points, and the third is the one that matters.* A listener cannot look back, so the speaker tells them where they are.

**Rhythm.** Shorter sentences than an article; the triplet; the repeated opening; the question the room will answer; the pause written as a short sentence. A speech that reads aloud badly is not a speech.

**The ending.** A call: what the room should do, think or ask for. The last sentence of a speech is the one the room repeats.

**What not to write.** Stage directions, *pauses for applause*; a title; a reference list. The words are the whole performance.

The audience is present, and enrolled at once
Three points, and the third is the one that matters

steps.title: Register within a form: who exactly is reading
steps.body:
A form narrows the register; the named audience fixes it. Two articles can differ more than an article and a letter.

**Two articles.** For a school magazine: *Nobody remembers who had the biggest car in the year above.* For a broadsheet: *The advice given to most sixteen-year-olds about careers is, in one respect, exactly wrong.* Same position, different reader: the first assumes a shared world and a taste for the quick; the second assumes an adult who wants a case.

**Two letters.** To a head teacher: *Dear Mrs Okafor, I am writing about …* To a friend who is choosing a job, if a task ever asked for it: *You asked me what I would do, so here it is.* The reader decides the distance.

**Two speeches.** To a year group: hands up. To a governors' meeting: *Good evening. I have been asked to speak for the students, and I will take five minutes.*

**The check.** Read the first paragraph and ask who it sounds as if it is for. If the answer is the examiner, start again.

steps.title: Dress the argument
steps.body:
Take a position you can argue in one sentence: *Schools should start at ten.* Write the first paragraph three times, in ten minutes: as a letter to the head teacher, as an article for a local newspaper, as a speech to a school assembly.

Then check each against its form: the letter has a title, a purpose and a request; the article has a headline and a hook; the speech addresses the room and has no greeting. And check each against its reader: who does it sound as if it is for?

steps.title: Assuredly: the form worn lightly
steps.body:
The top descriptor wants the register assuredly matched. In a form, assured means the conventions are present and the reader does not notice them: the letter sounds like a letter because of its voice, not because of a sign-off bolted on.

**Conventions as voice.** The head teacher is addressed by title and then spoken to as a person who can be persuaded; the room is enrolled in the first line and never let go; the magazine's reader is treated as someone who shares the writer's world and will enjoy being talked to like it.

**Conventions as structure.** The article's return to its headline; the letter's request restated in the last paragraph; the speech's call that echoes its opening. Structural features used with intent, in the form's own terms.

**The seams hidden.** No addresses, no dates, no subheadings every four lines, no stage directions. The conventions that earn are the ones a reader hears.

**And the same five minutes.** A speech tempts sentences without full stops; a letter tempts *would of* and *your* for *you're* under pressure of politeness. Check the demarcation and the sign-off.

steps.title: The forms in one page
steps.body:
The task names a form and an audience every time, and the form is the register's first decision.

- **Article:** a headline that promises the position; a hooking first paragraph; paragraphs that argue; a closing line that returns or asks. The publication sets the voice.
- **Letter:** a greeting with the title; purpose and request in the first paragraph; courteous, firm; a sign-off that matches the greeting. No addresses or dates.
- **Speech:** the room addressed and enrolled; signposting; rhythm for the ear; a closing call; no greeting or sign-off, no stage directions.
- **Underneath all three:** the same plan, a position, reasons, the counter-argument met, an ending that asks.
- **The named reader fixes the register** within the form; the first paragraph should sound as if it is for them.
- **Assured** means the conventions heard, not seen, and the same five minutes to check.

The argument itself has its own topic.

questions.prompt: Write the opening paragraph of the same argument, that schools should start at ten, three times: as a letter to the head teacher, as an article for a local newspaper, and as a speech to a school assembly. Each opening should state or imply the position and sound as if it is for its reader.
questions.solution:
Letter. Dear Mrs Okafor, I am writing to propose that the school day begin at ten rather than half past eight, and to ask you to consider the evidence for it before the next timetable is set. I know the change would be difficult to arrange, and I want to answer that difficulty as well as to make the case.

Article. Headline: Let them sleep. First paragraph: At half past eight on a Tuesday, four hundred teenagers file into a building to do the hardest thinking of their day at the hour their bodies are least able to do it. Everybody in the building knows this. The science has known it for twenty years. The only thing that has not changed is the bell.

Speech. Hands up if you were awake before seven this morning. Keep them up if you wanted to be. Now keep them up if the first thing you did in this building today was something you will remember tomorrow. I will not turn round. I already know.

questions.modelAnswer:
Letter. Dear Mrs Okafor, I am writing to propose that the school day begin at ten rather than half past eight, and to ask you to consider the evidence for it before the next timetable is set. I know the change would be difficult to arrange, and I want to answer that difficulty as well as to make the case.

Article. Headline: Let them sleep. First paragraph: At half past eight on a Tuesday, four hundred teenagers file into a building to do the hardest thinking of their day at the hour their bodies are least able to do it. Everybody in the building knows this. The science has known it for twenty years. The only thing that has not changed is the bell.

Speech. Hands up if you were awake before seven this morning. Keep them up if you wanted to be. Now keep them up if the first thing you did in this building today was something you will remember tomorrow. I will not turn round. I already know.

questions.prompt: Write a complete letter of about 400 words to your head teacher arguing for or against a proposal that the school day should end at half past two. Use the conventions of a formal letter, worn lightly: the title, the purpose and request first, two reasons, the objection met courteously, the request restated, the matching sign-off.
questions.solution:
Dear Mrs Okafor,

I am writing about the proposal to end the school day at half past two from September, and to ask you to keep the day as it is. I understand the reasons for the proposal, and I want to answer them, but I also want to put the students' case, because I do not think it has been heard.

The first reason is that the hour we would lose is the hour we can least afford. Period five is when most of us do the work that needs a teacher in the room: the practical, the essay planned with help, the problem worked through on the board. Homework can replace the reading and the practice; it cannot replace the person who sees where we are going wrong. Cutting the day cuts the hour in which we are taught, and keeps the hours in which we are told.

The second reason is who the change would fall on. For a student with a quiet room, a desk and a parent who did the subject, an extra hour at home is a small thing. For a student with a shift at the shop, a younger brother to collect and a phone that is also the family computer, it is an hour of school taken away and nothing put in its place. The school has said for years that it wants to narrow that gap. A shorter day widens it.

I expect you will say that the change saves money, and that the money is needed. That is true, and I would not pretend otherwise. But a saving that is paid for by the students it is meant to serve is not a saving; it is a transfer, from the school's budget to our futures, and I do not think that is the exchange the school wants to make.

I would ask you, then, to keep the day as it is, and to let the students' council put its own proposals for savings to you; I would be glad to explain our view in person at any time that suits you.

Yours sincerely,

Amara Bello, Year 11

questions.prompt: A task asks for a speech to a governors' meeting. A student writes as if to a year group, with hands up and slang. What is the problem?
questions.solution: The named audience fixes the register within the form. Good evening, I have been asked to speak for the students, enrols governors; hands up enrols a year group. The descriptors match register to audience, and a speech to the wrong room has mismatched it.

markScheme.description: The form is right and the audience is wrong: governors are enrolled differently from students, and the register is matched to the audience named

options: The problem is only that slang loses marks on AO6
Nothing: a speech is a speech, and the same one can be given to any room, since the examiners mark the argument and not the audience
The form is right and the audience is wrong: governors are enrolled differently from students, and the register is matched to the audience named
The student should have written a letter, since governors prefer letters

questions.prompt: A student says: 'Layout is what shows the examiner I know the form, so I put addresses on my letter and subheadings in my article.' What is the better account?
questions.solution: Assured use of a form is heard in the voice and the structure. Layout bolted on is the sign of a writer performing the form rather than using it, and it costs time that the argument and the check need.

markScheme.description: The conventions that earn are the ones a reader hears, the title and the request, the hook and the return, the room addressed; addresses and subheadings every four lines are seams

options: Addresses are required by the mark scheme, and a letter without them scores zero for content and organisation however good the rest is
The student is right, and more layout means more marks, because the examiners check each form against a list of its features and count them
Layout is all that is marked on AO5, so the argument does not matter and the time is better spent on the addresses and the subheadings

examTechnique.body:
**Read the form off the task, then the audience.** Article, letter or speech; a school magazine, a head teacher, a year group. Both decide the register, and the register is judged from the first line.

**Article:** a headline that promises the position; a hooking first paragraph; a closing line that returns or asks.

**Letter:** the title; the purpose and request in the first paragraph; courteous and firm; the request restated; Yours sincerely for a name, Yours faithfully for Sir or Madam. No addresses or dates.

**Speech:** the room addressed and enrolled; signposting; sentences for the ear; a closing call. No greeting, no sign-off, no stage directions.

**Underneath all three, the same plan,** and the same five minutes to check.
examinerErrors: Writing an essay when the task named an article, a letter or a speech, so the register is nobody's.
A speech with a greeting and a sign-off, or a letter without a matching sign-off.
Address blocks and dates on a letter, which earn nothing and cost time.
A headline that names the topic rather than promising the position.
A speech that reads aloud badly: long sentences, no signposting, no call at the end.
The right form for the wrong reader: hands up to a governors' meeting, a chat to a head teacher.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 piece knows its form and its reader from its first line and wears the form lightly: the letter has its title, its purpose and request first, its courtesy and its matching sign-off, and no seams; the article has a headline that promises, a first paragraph that hooks and a last line that returns; the speech enrols the room, signposts its turns, is written for the ear and ends on a sentence the room can repeat. Underneath, the same argument: a position, reasons, the counter-argument met in the same voice, an ending that asks. And it is checked, because the form's rhythm tempts the punctuation.
